idiom_name: class with #private sealed map + node:crypto AES-256-GCM + toJSON()/inspect hooks
implementation_notes: JavaScript serializes objects by walking their own enumerable properties, so the transfer object is a class that keeps protected pairs in a #private field, seals them with an authenticated cipher from node:crypto (createCipheriv('aes-256-gcm') plus getAuthTag) and controls every rendering path: toJSON() for JSON.stringify and the Node inspect symbol (Symbol.for('nodejs.util.inspect.custom')) for console.log and interpolation. What replaces the classic structure: the #private field plus those serialization hooks replace the class's protected map and masked list. Note that WebCrypto (crypto.subtle) is asynchronous and returns ArrayBuffers, so a synchronous log or toString path cannot use it and browser sealing is inherently an async operation.
pitfalls: toJSON is honoured by JSON.stringify but not by spread ({...obj}), Object.assign, structuredClone or libraries that copy own enumerable properties - #private fields are the only hard barrier, so plaintext must never live in a normal property.

Each runtime has its own inspection hook: Node's console.log uses util.inspect.custom, browsers use devtools formatting, and JSON.stringify uses toJSON - all three paths have to be handled or the masked map shows up in one of them.

GCM IVs and tags travel with the ciphertext and an IV must never repeat under one key; Node removed createCipher/createDecipher precisely because of weak IV generation, so use randomBytes and getAuthTag rather than reviving old snippets.
JavaScript strings are immutable and cannot be zeroed; Buffer copies can be filled with zeros and discarded, but any string conversion of a secret survives until garbage collection.
